newsitem.title: USA: U.S. wholesalers' stocks jump sharply in June.
newsitem.headline: U.S. wholesalers' stocks jump sharply in June.

text.p: Stocks of unsold goods on wholesalers' shelves jumped at the sharpest rate in more than 15 years during June, the Commerce Department said on Thursday, partly because of a buildup in inventories of new cars.

Total inventories climbed 1.9 percent to a seasonally adjusted $263.93 billion in June, much higher than the revised 0.4 percent gain posted for May. Previously, the department said May inventories had gained 0.2 percent.
The June inventories increase was the largest for any month since April 1982, when they rose 2 percent, the department said.

Total sales by wholesalers rose only 0.3 percent in June to a seasonally adjusted $210.69 billion after being revised to show no change in May instead of a 0.2 percent gain as the department previously estimated.

As a result, wholesalers had 1.25 months' worth of goods on hand in June, the highest level since October last year, when they also had 1.25 months' worth. The so-called inventories-to-sales ratio, which measures how long it would take to sell existing inventories at current prices, was up from 1.23 months' worth in May.

One of the biggest increases in inventories was for new cars, which gained 5.1 percent from May to a value of $28.25 billion in June. Stocks of professional and commercial equipment and supplies grew 3.1 percent to $22.84 billion in May.
Department officials said the 5.1 percent jump in auto inventories was the sharpest since a 5.5 percent increase in January 1991, shortly before the last recession ended.

Some of the buildup in total stocks may be voluntary, in anticipation of a rebound in consumer spending during the third quarter. While spending fell off in the second quarter, slowing the pace of overall economic growth from the first quarter, strong job creation in July, as well as high levels of consumer confidence, are forecast to bolster spending in the current third quarter.

The Federal Reserve, in its latest Beige Book survey of national economic activitiy issued on Wednesday, said the tempo of consumer spending picked up in June and July for most goods except for new cars.
But many car manufacturers began offering sales incentives late in July, which resulted in a sales pickup, according to industry reports.
